sections.heading: The legal rule
sections.body:
358. (1) The Indian Penal Code is hereby repealed
(2) Notwithstanding the repeal of the Code referred to in sub-section (1), it shall not affect,—
(a) the previous operation of the Code so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; or
(b) any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the Code so repealed; or
(c) any penalty, or punishment incurred in respect of any offences committed against the Code so repealed; or
(d) any investigation or remedy in respect of any such penalty, or punishment; or
(e) any proceeding, investigation or remedy in respect of any such penalty or punishment as aforesaid, and any such proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced, and any such penalty may be imposed as if that Code had not been repealed
(3) Notwithstanding such repeal, anything done or any action taken under the said Code shall be deemed to have been done or taken under the corresponding provisions of this Sanhita
(4) The mention of particular matters in sub-section (2) shall not be held to prejudice or affect the general application of section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 with regard to the effect of the repeal

hypotheticals.question: Whether BNS s. 358 (Repeal and savings) applies, and how structured written arguments should be framed.
hypotheticals.analysis:
Step 1 — Identify the provision. The correct current-law cite is BNS s. 358 (Repeal and savings), Chapter XX — Repeal and Savings.
Step 2 — State the legal test in your own words, then list the ingredients:
   (1) (1) The Indian Penal Code is hereby repealed
   (2) (2) Notwithstanding the repeal of the Code referred to in sub-section
   (3) (1), it shall not affect,—
   (4) (a) the previous operation of the Code so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; or
   (5) (b) any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the Code so repealed; or
   (6) (c) any penalty, or punishment incurred in respect of any offences committed against the Code so repealed; or
   (7) (d) any investigation or remedy in respect of any such penalty, or punishment; or
   (8) (e) any proceeding, investigation or remedy in respect of any such penalty or punishment as aforesaid, and any such proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced, and any such penalty may be imposed as if that Code had not been repealed
Step 3 — Check limitations, provisos and the rest of the Chapter so you do not apply s. 358 in a vacuum.
Step 4 — Map each fact to an ingredient. Write “this fact proves ingredient (a)” or “this fact is missing, so the section is not made out”.
Step 5 — Conclude. If every essential ingredient is proved and no exception covers the case, BNS s. 358 applies. If any essential ingredient fails, say so and stop. Do not invent a different section to save the answer.

questionsAndAnswers.question: Legal Assessment & Statutory Note: BNS s. 358 (Repeal and savings)
questionsAndAnswers.answer:
Introduction. BNS s. 358 deals with Repeal and savings. It sits in Chapter XX — Repeal and Savings of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. After 1 July 2024 this is the current-law citation for this offence / definition / punishment.

Meaning. Repeal and savings. The Indian Penal Code, 1860 is repealed. Anything done, any right, privilege, obligation, liability, penalty or punishment under the IPC, and any investigation or proceeding in respect of an IPC offence, continues. Offences committed before 1 July 2024 are IPC offences.

Legal rule. In student language: BNS s. 358 is the rule on “Repeal and savings”. The section provides that (1) The Indian Penal Code is hereby repealed. Do not stop at the heading. An examiner awards marks for the ingredients, the explanations and the illustrations, not for writing the title alone.

Essential ingredients. An authoritative analysis must list them, not hide them in one paragraph:
1. (1) The Indian Penal Code is hereby repealed
2. (2) Notwithstanding the repeal of the Code referred to in sub-section
3. (1), it shall not affect,—
4. (a) the previous operation of the Code so repealed or anything duly done or suffered thereunder; or
5. (b) any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred under the Code so repealed; or
6. (c) any penalty, or punishment incurred in respect of any offences committed against the Code so repealed; or
7. (d) any investigation or remedy in respect of any such penalty, or punishment; or
8. (e) any proceeding, investigation or remedy in respect of any such penalty or punishment as aforesaid, and any such proceeding or remedy may be instituted, continued or enforced, and any such penalty may be imposed as if that Code had not been repealed

Illustration. Give one short original example (label it as an example) and apply the ingredients.

Limitations. Apply only the conditions written in s. 358. Do not import a defence from a different chapter unless the question requires it.

Conclusion. BNS s. 358 is the complete current-law heading for Repeal and savings. Define, list ingredients, use an illustration, note any explanation or exception, apply, cite. That is a complete statutory structure.

Comprehensive Written Submissions. Deepen the doctrinal synthesis with four foundational layers.

Layer 1 — Place the section in the Chapter. The IPC goes. Offences committed before 1 July 2024 stay under the old Code.. Show why this heading sits where it sits.

Layer 2 — Work a second, slightly harder hypothetical. Change one ingredient and show why the section then fails.

Layer 3 — Analytical comment. Explain a condition, a proviso, or a practical difficulty in applying s. 358. Do not invent case names.



Layer 5 — Application and current-law close. Apply the test to the problem facts in IRAC form (Issue, Rule, Application, Conclusion). Close with: “The governing citation on or after 1 July 2024 is BNS s. 358.”

cases.name: Navtej Singh Johar v. Union of India
cases.holding: IPC 377 read down for consenting adults. BNS does not re-enact 377. Consensual same-sex intimacy is not an offence; non-consensual male rape is a legislative gap.

cases.name: Joseph Shine v. Union of India
cases.holding: Adultery (IPC 497) struck down. BNS does not revive it. Marital infidelity is not, by itself, a crime.

examTips: Cite BNS s. 358 for offences on or after 1 July 2024.
Ingredients first, illustration second, application third, conclusion last.
Date of the offence, not date of the FIR, decides IPC vs BNS on substance.

learningObjectives: Master the legal effect of the repeal of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 by Section 358(1) BNS.
Analyze the statutory savings under Section 358(2) preserving previous operations, acquired rights, accrued liabilities, penalties, and pending investigations.
Understand the deeming provision under Section 358(3) and the statutory application of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 under Section 358(4).
Evaluate transitional criminal liability: determining whether pre-1 July 2024 acts are governed by the IPC or the BNS under Article 20(1) of the Constitution.
enhancement.definition: BNS s. 358 governs the formal repeal of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 and enacts comprehensive statutory savings. It provides that the repeal of the 1860 Code shall not affect its previous operation, anything duly done or suffered thereunder, any right, privilege, obligation or liability acquired, accrued or incurred, or any penalty, punishment, forfeiture, investigation, or legal proceeding in respect thereof, which may be instituted, continued, or enforced as if the IPC had not been repealed.
enhancement.legalPrinciple: The constitutional and statutory principle of non-retroactivity of criminal law (Article 20(1)) and legislative continuity (Section 6, General Clauses Act, 1897). A repeal does not obliterate vested rights, accrued penal liabilities, or ongoing investigations for offences committed prior to the commencement of the new penal code.
statutoryFramework: Chapter XIX — Of Criminal Intimidation, Insult, Annoyance, Defamation, etc., and Repeal, BNS s. 358.
Sub-section (1): Express repeal of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 (Act No. 45 of 1860).
Sub-section (2)(a)-(e): Specific savings saving previous operation, acquired rights, accrued liabilities, punishments, and pending proceedings/remedies.
Sub-section (3): Deeming fiction that actions taken under the IPC correspond to actions under the BNS.
Sub-section (4): Express preservation of the general application of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
essentialIngredients: The formal statutory repeal of the Indian Penal Code, 1860 with effect from 1 July 2024.
Offence, act, omission, or proceeding occurring prior to 1 July 2024 falling under the temporal domain of the repealed IPC.
Preservation of accrued criminal liabilities and punishments: offences committed prior to 1 July 2024 remain punishable strictly under the IPC.
Continuation of legal proceedings, investigations, and remedies as if the IPC had not been repealed, without violating Article 20(1) ex-post facto prohibitions.
enhancement.detailedExplanation:
Section 358 BNS is the pivotal transitional bridge connecting the historic Indian Penal Code, 1860 with the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023. It performs two distinct legal functions: first, under sub-section (1), it repeals the 164-year-old Indian Penal Code; second, under sub-sections (2) through (4), it prevents a legal vacuum by preserving the entire apparatus of substantive liability for acts committed prior to the midnight of 30 June 2024.

Under Article 20(1) of the Constitution of India, no person can be convicted of an offence except for violation of a law in force at the time of the commission of the act charged as an offence, nor be subjected to a penalty greater than that which might have been inflicted under the law in force at that time. Consequently, Section 358(2)(b) and (c) ensure that if an act was committed on or before 30 June 2024, the accused must be charged, tried, and sentenced under the provisions of the IPC (e.g., Section 302 IPC or Section 376 IPC), even if the FIR is registered or the trial commences after 1 July 2024. Conversely, acts committed on or after 1 July 2024 must be charged exclusively under the corresponding provisions of the BNS.

Sub-section (3) provides an administrative deeming fiction: actions taken under the old Code (such as statutory rules, appointments, or notifications) are deemed to have been taken under the corresponding provisions of the BNS. Sub-section (4) clarifies that the specific enumeration in sub-section (2) does not restrict the wide protective umbrella of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897.
examples: Teaching illustration (Pre-commencement offence): Accused A commits forgery on 15 June 2024. The victim discovers the fraud and lodges an FIR on 10 July 2024 (after BNS commencement). Under Section 358(2)(c) and (e) BNS read with Article 20(1), the FIR and chargesheet must be registered under Section 468 of the Indian Penal Code, 1860, not under BNS Section 336. Section 358 saves the liability incurred under the repealed IPC.

Teaching illustration (Post-commencement offence): Accused B commits theft on 5 July 2024. The police erroneously register an FIR citing Section 379 IPC. The charge is defective because the IPC was repealed on 1 July 2024 under Section 358(1). The offence must be charged under Section 303(2) of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023.
distinctions: BNS s. 358 vs BNSS s. 531: BNS s. 358 governs substantive penal liability and the repeal of the IPC 1860, whereas BNSS s. 531 governs procedural transition and the repeal of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.

BNS s. 358 vs Section 6 General Clauses Act: Section 358 enacts specific statutory savings for the BNS, but sub-section (4) explicitly preserves the general principles of Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 to prevent omissions.
problemApplication: Issue: Whether an accused who committed an act of cheating on 28 June 2024 can be charged and sentenced under Section 318 BNS in an FIR registered on 15 July 2024.

Rule: Under BNS s. 358(2) read with Article 20(1) of the Constitution, offences committed prior to 1 July 2024 remain substantive offences under the repealed Indian Penal Code, 1860; substantive provisions of the BNS cannot be applied retrospectively.
Application: The alleged acts of cheating occurred on 28 June 2024, prior to the commencement of the BNS. The liability was accrued under Section 420 IPC.
Conclusion: The charge under Section 318 BNS is legally unsustainable; the court must direct the alteration of the charge to Section 420 IPC pursuant to Section 358(2) BNS.

shortAnswer: State that Section 358(1) BNS repeals the Indian Penal Code, 1860 with effect from 1 July 2024.
Explain that Section 358(2) saves prior rights, accrued liabilities, punishments, and ongoing proceedings.
Highlight the constitutional nexus with Article 20(1): pre-July 2024 acts are governed by the IPC.

Detailed analysis of Section 358(1) and the five specific savings clauses under Section 358(2)(a)–(e).
Constitutional mandate: Article 20(1) and the prohibition of ex-post facto penal law.
Deeming fiction under Section 358(3) and interaction with Section 6 of the General Clauses Act under 358(4).

Exhaustive clause-by-clause dissection of BNS Section 358: Sub-sections (1), (2), (3), and (4).
Constitutional interface: Detailed examination of Article 20(1), double jeopardy under 20(2), and fair trial under Article 21.

Litigation pitfalls: Incorrect section citation in post-commencement FIRs for pre-commencement crimes and judicial curative powers.
Structured IRAC problem resolution and overarching conclusion on legislative transition.

keyTakeaways: Section 358(1) BNS formally repeals the Indian Penal Code, 1860.
Section 358(2) strictly preserves liabilities and punishments for offences committed prior to 1 July 2024 under the IPC.
Substantive BNS provisions apply prospectively to offences committed on or after 1 July 2024.
Section 6 of the General Clauses Act, 1897 continues to apply in full force by virtue of Section 358(4).
